summary: Describes how to spread flows across equal-cost multipath routes in a softwire mesh. The payloads in a softwire often contain separate identifiable flows, and balancing them can use available links better.

eli5.summary: If many cars travel in one convoy tunnel, it is better to split them over several roads. This explains how to do that.

questions: what is a load-balancing block sub-tlv
how does ecmp work with softwire tunnels
what is the l2tpv3 session id used for in load balancing
what is the gre key used for in load balancing
subtitle: A small BGP extension that lets core routers spread tunneled traffic over equal-cost paths.

tldr.problem: Packets inside a softwire tunnel look identical to core routers, because only the outer header is visible. Many separate flows therefore get pinned to a single equal-cost path.
tldr.mechanism: A new Load-Balancing Block sub-TLV tells ingress routers how many leading bits of the tunnel's load-balancing field (L2TPv3 Session ID or GRE Key) are fixed. The ingress fills the remaining bits with a per-flow value, so core routers see more variety.
tldr.outcome: Softwire mesh traffic can be balanced across equal-cost paths about as well as it would be without encapsulation. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9012.

today: RFC 5640 is a Proposed Standard from August 2009 and is updated by RFC 9012. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Problem: Hidden Flows in a Tunnel
sections.content:
A Softwire mesh service carries payloads between routers using tunnels. The RFC's abstract points out that these payloads often carry a number of identifiable, distinct flows, and that it can be desirable to spread those flows over the equal cost multiple paths (ECMPs) in the network.

The catch is that only the ingress and egress routers can interpret the payload. A core router choosing among equal-cost paths looks only at the encapsulating header, which offers much less entropy than the payload or the inner header would.

The RFC's setup is a router R1 that encapsulates a packet P into a softwire bound for R3, with R2 on the shortest path between them. R2 has equal-cost paths to R3, and the goal is for R2 to choose among them using the full entropy of packet P.
sections.eli5: Everything in the tunnel wears one outer label, so the road-sorting routers cannot tell the cars apart and send them all the same way.

sections.title: The Load-Balancing Field
sections.content:
The idea is to carry a signature of the inner header in the encapsulation header, so core routers see more entropy. The signature rides in one field of the encapsulation header, which the RFC calls the load-balancing field.

The field depends on the tunnel type. For L2TPv3 over IP (RFC 3931) it is the Session Identifier (Session ID). For GRE (RFC 2784) it is the Key field from RFC 2890, if present.

The mechanism assumes core routers include the load-balancing field in their flow definition. The RFC calls this an obvious and generic capability: for L2TPv3-over-IP, the Session ID sits at the same well-known constant offset as the TCP/UDP ports in the encapsulating header.

The Encapsulation SAFI from RFC 5512 is extended so that a contiguous block of the load-balancing field is bound to the softwire advertised by a BGP next-hop. For each inner flow, the ingress Provider Edge (PE) selects one value from the block. That keeps packets of a flow in order and still adds entropy across flows.
sections.eli5: The tunnel already has a number on its outside. Instead of using one number for everything, the sender picks from a small set of numbers, using a different one for each conversation.

sections.title: The Load-Balancing Block Sub-TLV
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new sub-TLV for the Tunnel Encapsulation Attribute of RFC 5512. It is called the Load-Balancing Block sub-TLV, and it MAY be included in any Encapsulation SAFI UPDATE message where load-balancing is desired.

Its sub-TLV type is 5 and its length is 2 octets. The value is the length of the block in bits, and it MUST NOT exceed the size of the load-balancing field. The RFC compares this to variable-length subnet masking: the block is the initial sequence of that many bits taken from the load-balancing field.

If no load-balancing field is signaled, for example GRE without a Key, the sub-TLV MUST NOT be included.

There is a trade-off. A smaller value leaves more room for per-flow identification, which gives better entropy and less polarization when mapping flows to ECMP paths. But it consumes more Session IDs or GRE Keys, which can mean fewer supported services. A typical deployment has to arbitrate between the two.
sections.eli5: The number says how much of the label is fixed and how much the sender may change. Changing more of it spreads cars better, but uses up more labels.

sections.title: Worked Example: Session ID 0x1234ABCD
sections.content:
Suppose a softwire is set up between R1 and R3 using the L2TPv3-over-IP tunnel type. R3 advertises Session ID 0x1234ABCD in the encapsulation sub-TLV and also includes the Load-Balancing Block sub-TLV with the value 24.

  • An ingress router that does not understand the sub-TLV keeps using Session ID 0x1234ABCD for all packets.
  • An ingress router that does understand it takes the first 24 bits (0x1234AB) as the block and fills the lower-order 8 bits with a per-flow identifier. The RFC suggests deriving it from the inner packet's source and destination addresses and TCP/UDP ports. This preserves per-flow ordering.

The same approach applies to GRE, where the Key plays the role of the Session ID. If an egress router does not support the sub-TLV, the softwire keeps working with a single load-balancing field that all ingress routers use.
sections.eli5: If the label is 1234ABCD, the sender keeps the first part fixed and swaps the last bit of it for a different value for each conversation. Old equipment simply ignores all this and uses the plain label.

sections.title: Tunnel Types and Encapsulation
sections.content:
The sub-TLV applies to tunnel types that define a load-balancing field. The RFC defines one for tunnel type 1 (L2TPv3 over IP), where it is the Session ID, and for tunnel type 2 (GRE), where it is the GRE Key. It does not define one for the IP-in-IP tunnel type (tunnel type 7). Future tunnel types that want to use the sub-TLV MUST define a load-balancing field that is part of the encapsulating header.

For L2TPv3 there is an extra rule. An egress router that includes the sub-TLV MUST encode the Session ID so that its most significant bits, after extracting the block, are non-zero, so a non-zero Session ID is always created.

Other encapsulation fields are not affected. If an optional L2TPv3 cookie is in the encapsulation sub-TLV, it applies to all the Session ID values the ingress derives from the block.
sections.eli5: Only tunnel types that have a suitable label field can play this game, and everything else about the tunnel stays as it was.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: IANA assigned the value 5 to the Load-Balancing Block sub-TLV in the BGP Tunnel Encapsulation Attribute Sub-TLVs registry, a number space created with the publication of RFC 5512.
sections.eli5: The official list of sub-label types got a new entry, number 5, for this feature.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC adds only a new sub-TLV to the BGP Tunnel Encapsulation Attribute. Security considerations for the BGP Encapsulation SAFI and that attribute are covered in RFC 5512, and the RFC states that there are no additional security risks introduced by this design.
sections.eli5: This is a small add-on to an existing system, so the safety rules of that system already cover it.
